extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational humor, psycholinguistics, NLP, and writers/comedians interested in lexical humor
extracted.subtask_description: A normative dataset and guidance for assessing or choosing individual English words by how humorous they are in isolation (4,997 words rated on a 1–5 funniness scale). Useful for word-level humor scoring, computational features, and informing lexical choices in comedic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-level funniness rating (1–5 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale: 1 (humorless) to 5 (humorous). 4,997 English words were rated by 821 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants (each rated 211 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary metric: per-word mean funniness ratings. The dataset overlaps with other normed pools (arousal, valence, concreteness, age-of-acquisition, reaction-time databases), and includes per-word demographic breakdowns. Use as a lookup table to score words in texts or as numerical features for models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse word frequency predicts funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest empirical correlate with humor rating is inverse word frequency (r = -0.42 with British National Corpus frequencies): less common words tend to be funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat low frequency as a robust, large effect when evaluating or choosing comic words. Familiar/high-frequency words tend to be unfunny. Use frequency measures (e.g., BNC) to estimate lexical funniness tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations for why low frequency increases funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Several plausible mechanisms: surprise (rare words violate expected vocabulary), distinctiveness (stand out and attract attention), phonetic markedness (unusual phonological properties), and cultural loadings (slangy, archaic, technical, or playful register).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the frequency rule, consider these mechanisms—e.g., choose words that create mild surprise or are register-marked. These mechanisms can guide deliberate word choice beyond raw frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic/iconic correlates of funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific phonological features correlate with higher funniness: voiceless plosives (/k/, /p/, /t/), bilabial sounds (/b/, /p/, /m/), reduplication (e.g., booby, bebop), and long vowel + plosive endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer words containing these phonetic features when multiple synonyms exist. Follow-up work links these sound patterns to perceived humor; use phonological analysis as an additional selection criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduplication and playful sound structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Words with reduplication or playful internal repetition (booby, bebop, tinkle) tend to be funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor reduplicated forms or those with repetitive rhythmic/sonic patterns for heightened lexical comic effect, especially in line-final or highlighted positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic predictors are weak (valence/arousal/concreteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valence (positive/negative emotional tone), arousal, and concreteness show only weak correlations with funniness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on emotional tone or concreteness alone to predict funniness; funniness is largely an independent lexical dimension. Use these semantic measures as secondary information, not primary predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical principles for choosing comic words
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing words for a comic line: pick the less common synonym; pick words with humor-correlated phonemes (k-sounds especially); pick concrete, picturable, low-register words over abstract/formal ones; pick words with reduplication or playful sound structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this checklist when multiple lexical choices are available. Small lexical swaps (to lower-frequency, phonologically marked words) can increase perceived funniness of a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lexically un-funny words in climactic positions
rubrics_metrics.description: High-frequency abstract nouns and lexically un-funny words should especially be avoided at climactic positions in a joke or utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting punchlines or climaxes, prioritize lexically-funny words; placing unfunny, formal, or high-frequency words at those positions can blunt the comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: excludes context, compositional, and joke-level effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset measures words in isolation and excludes context effects, compositional interactions between words, and joke-level funniness; word-level ratings do not directly predict joke success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these norms only as one component of humor analysis or creation. Always consider context, sequence, and higher-level compositional mechanisms when evaluating or writing jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for applying the norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested diagnostic questions: Does the joke use lexically-funny words where there is choice? Does the joke avoid lexically un-funny words (especially high-frequency abstract nouns) at climactic positions? Is the comic word low-frequency, phonetically marked, reduplicated, or k-containing? Does substituting a synonym change the comic effect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a quick evaluation checklist to spot lexical improvements. Perform synonym substitution tests to evaluate potential gains in funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset enables word-level humor scoring and computational features
rubrics_metrics.description: The norms can be used to score any text by lookup and to provide features in computational humor models; they also enable cross-cultural and dialect comparisons (e.g., American vs British vs Singapore English ratings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate mean word funniness, demographic splits, and phonetic features as model inputs. Validate models against joke-level outcomes cautiously due to noted limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic breakdowns and subgroup analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset includes demographic breakdowns by gender, age, and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider subgroup differences when using norms for targeted audiences or cross-population comparisons; apply demographic-specific ratings where appropriate rather than a single aggregate score.
